title: Exploring how things work
keyIdea: Everyday things have parts, and each part does a job. Press a torch button and the light comes on. Turn a tap handle more and more water comes out. Wind a toy's key and its spring makes it go. Pull a zip's tab and the two sides join. Squeeze a peg and its mouth opens. To find out how something works, try one part at a time and watch what happens: that is cause and effect.

kid: Things have parts. Each part has a job. A torch has a button. Press it and the light comes on. Press it again and the light goes off.
Some parts turn. Turn a tap a little, and a little water comes out. Turn it more, and more water comes out. Turn it back, and it stops.
A wind-up toy has a key. Turn the key and a spring inside gets tight. Let go and the toy walks. Turn the key more, and it walks further. It is not magic. The spring makes it go.
How does a thing work? Try one part. Watch what it does. Then try the next part. Ask a grown-up first if it is hot, sharp or plugged in.
adult: Development Matters, the guidance for England's Early Years Foundation Stage, lists 'Explore how things work' for 3- and 4-year-olds in Understanding the World. The skill is noticing cause and effect: I do this to this part, and that happens. It feeds later science, such as pushes and pulls, simple circuits and asking questions, and early design and technology, where children take things apart to see how they work.

Pick safe things with one clear moving part: a torch switch, a tap, a wind-up toy, a zip, a clothes peg, a jar lid, a door handle. Let your child try first, then talk about it: what did you do, which part moved, what happened. Words to use: press, turn, twist, pull, squeeze, wind, button, handle, spring, switch, on, off, more, less.

Common mistakes are explanations like 'the toy wants to walk' or 'it's magic'. Young children often give objects feelings or treat a result as magic. Gently replace these with the part that caused it: 'you wound the spring'. Another slip is thinking a toy stops because it is tired or sad, not because the spring has run down. Be careful to keep this hands-on but safe: no plug sockets, hot taps or sharp blades.

In the lab your child presses a torch button on and off, turns a tap a little and a lot to fill a cup, winds a toy once and then three times to see it go further, pulls a zip up by its tab, and squeezes a peg to hang three socks.

familyTip: Go on a 'how does it work?' hunt at home. Find three things with a part that moves: a light switch, a bottle top, a peg. For each one, ask 'What do you think will happen?' before your child tries it.

visual.caption: Do you press it or turn it? Drag each thing into a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: press a torch button, turn a tap a little and a lot, wind up a toy, pull a zip and squeeze a peg to find each part's job.

practice.prompt: Which part of a torch turns the light on?
practice.hint: Which part moves when you press it?
practice.explain: The button is the switch. Press it and the light comes on. Press it again and it goes off.

practice.prompt: You turn the toy's key {a} times. Then you turn it {b} more times. How many turns is that?
practice.hint: Start at {a} and count on {b} more turns.
practice.explain: {a} turns and {b} more turns make {=a+b} turns. More turns wind the spring tighter.

practice.prompt: There are {n} socks to hang up. Each sock needs 1 peg. How many pegs do you need?
practice.explain: One peg for each sock, so {n} socks need {n} pegs.

practice.prompt: You turn the tap more. What happens?
practice.hint: Turning back makes the water stop. What does turning more do?
practice.explain: Turning the tap handle more lets more water out. Turning it back makes less, then none.

pool.prompt: Why does a wind-up toy walk?
pool.hint: What did you do to the key before it walked?
pool.explain: Turning the key winds a spring inside. When you let go, the spring makes the toy walk.

pool.prompt: How do you open a peg?
pool.hint: Press the two long ends together.
pool.explain: Squeezing the ends opens the mouth. Let go and the spring shuts it tight.

pool.prompt: Which part of a zip do you pull?
pool.hint: It is the small part you can hold.
pool.explain: Pull the little tab. It moves the slider, and the slider joins the two sides.

pool.prompt: The toy stops walking. How can it walk again?
choices: Wait and it will go by itself
pool.hint: What made it walk the first time?
pool.explain: The spring has run down. Turn the key again to wind it up, and it will walk again.

pool.prompt: You wind the toy {a} times, then {b} times. How many more turns was the second go?
pool.hint: Start at {a} and count up to {b}.
pool.explain: From {a} up to {b} is {=b-a} more turns, so the second go walks further.

pool.prompt: There are {n} socks. You have pegged {k} on the line. How many still need a peg?
pool.hint: Start at {n} and take away the {k} that are hanging.
pool.explain: {n} take away {k} leaves {=n-k} socks still to peg.

pool.prompt: You do not know how a box opens. What is a good thing to do?
choices: Try one part and see what it does
pool.hint: How did you find out what the tap did?
pool.explain: Try one part gently, watch what happens, then try the next part. That is how you find out.

pool.prompt: You press a light switch. What happens?
choices: The light goes on or off
pool.hint: A switch is like the torch button.
pool.explain: A light switch turns the light on, or off if it was on. Each switch does one job.
